<reason>Side B won decisively by exposing a fatal contradiction at the heart of Side A's case and dismantling Side A's practical objections. Side A argued both that social media users instantly recognize commercial context and that requiring a spoken disclosure would destroy the "authenticity" of the video. Side B used its pressure questions and second rebuttal to show that if stating a pitch is paid ruins its authenticity, that authenticity depends on deceiving the viewer. When Side A tried to escape this trap in Rebuttal 2 by admitting that general skepticism "does not tell a viewer which product is paid" and that sponsors pay for a "perceived unmediated relationship," Side B capitalized on that concession in Closing to prove why explicit verbal and visual disclosures are necessary. Side B also cleanly refuted Side A's strawman that broadcast-level strictness requires scheduled commercial breaks and refuted the implausible claim that mega-influencers would cap or split their own audiences just to avoid disclosure rules.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's pressure question [B3.1] and follow-through in [B4.5-B4.7] and [B5.1-B5.2], which trapped Side A between claiming viewers already know content is commercial and claiming that saying "paid ad" aloud ruins the illusion of an unmediated relationship.</best_rebuttal>
